items.title: Anthropic's net revenue retention is ~900%. The best ever at IPO was Snowflake at 158%
items.idea: From the roadshow: a customer that spent $100 in a quarter last year now spends ~$900 in the same quarter. Snowflake's 158% was the previous record for an IPO. ~75% of revenue comes from ~12,000 customers spending $100K+. Usage-based revenue is 79%, subscriptions 21%, and the US is 71% of revenue.
items.angle: NRR of 900% is not SaaS land-and-expand. It is consumption, which is how a utility behaves. That brings utility-style cyclicality: usage revenue (79%) can contract as fast as it grows if token prices fall or budgets get cut.
items.tweetA: Snowflake IPO'd with 158% NRR and everyone called it the best software business ever. Anthropic is filing with ~900%. Either that's the most powerful land-and-expand in history, or we're mislabeling a utility bill as SaaS. $ANT
items.tweetB: 79% of Anthropic revenue is usage-based. That isn't a subscription moat, it's a meter. Meters go up 9x when budgets are loose and roll over fast when CFOs start counting tokens. Price the IPO on that.

items.title: Fortune 500 Claude customers spend <0.1% of total expenses on it. Even the top 10 are under 1%
items.idea: Anthropic's growth thesis is share of existing corporate spend, not new budgets. Today the average Fortune 500 customer puts under 0.1% of its total expenses toward Claude, and even the 10 biggest spenders are below 1%. More than half the Fortune 500 already spends over $100K.
items.angle: Read it against McKinsey's estimate (AI Street, same day) that token costs could hit 20% of bank labor costs. Going from 0.1% of opex to a labor-sized line item is the whole bull case, and it's also exactly what CFOs are now building teams to cap.
items.tweetA: Fortune 500 companies spend <0.1% of their opex on Claude. McKinsey says token costs could reach 20% of bank labor costs. The entire Anthropic IPO is a bet on which of those numbers wins.
items.tweetB: Bull case in one line: half the Fortune 500 already pays Anthropic $100K+, and the top-10 customers still spend under 1% of their costs on it. The distribution exists. The only question is the wallet.

items.title: Q3 revenue +1,127% vs compute costs +382%. 90% of Anthropic's new code is written by Claude
items.idea: Anthropic says 'compute multipliers' (research gains) let revenue grow ~3x faster than compute spend in Q3. Over 90% of code added to its codebase in Sept 2026 was written by Claude, and revenue per employee is up ~5x in a year. It trains and serves on Trainium, TPU, NVIDIA and AMD as one pool, routing each workload to the cheapest hardware, which the author calls a bear case for Nvidia margins. The IPO target was cut from ~$2T to ~$1.3T, with a $74 price referenced.
items.angle: On a day NVDA lost its CEO, the more durable risk to its margins is the biggest customers treating GPUs as interchangeable. Multi-silicon routing plus SemiAnalysis's call that >70% of 2028 capacity could be non-Nvidia point the same way.
items.tweetA: Anthropic: revenue +1,127%, compute cost +382%. That gap is the most important number in the S-1, because it means the model gets cheaper to run as it scales. Every other AI business plan assumes the opposite.
items.tweetB: Anthropic routes each workload to whichever chip is cheapest: Trainium, TPU, NVIDIA, AMD. When your largest customer runs a reverse auction across four vendors, your 75% gross margin is a negotiation, not a moat. $NVDA $AMZN $GOOGL

items.title: Jeff Booth runs an offline open-source model that would have been the world's best frontier model 4 months ago
items.idea: Booth runs a local, fully offline open-source model holding all of his own data ('a brain on his machine'). Four months ago that capability was the global frontier. His question: if a lab spends tens of billions to build a moat and the moat lasts four months, how does it ever earn the capex back?
items.angle: A 4-month half-life on frontier capability is the bear case for frontier-lab valuations ($ANT at ~$1.3T) and the bull case for edge hardware and memory. Compare with Anthropic's own pitch, where distribution and safety brand are the moat, not raw capability.
items.tweetA: Frontier model → laptop model in 4 months. If that's the depreciation schedule on a $10B training run, AI labs should be valued like fashion brands, not utilities. The moat has to be distribution, because the weights aren't one.
items.tweetB: Nobody prices the 'offline brain' scenario. A sovereign, local model on your own data with no API bill and no subscription. When that's good enough for 80% of tasks, the token meter stops. Watch memory and edge silicon, not cloud.

items.title: Through the NVDA meltdown, BTC sat at $74K with ETF outflows and gold slipped toward $3,970: no flight to hard assets
items.idea: Brunell notes Nvidia's board can remove the CEO by simple majority of 11 directors, with or without cause. Prediction markets had 88% odds Huang was gone by year-end, and NVDA was ~33% below its early-October peak (~$600B erased) before he resigned. Despite the concentration shock, BTC held ~$74K with ETF outflows still running and gold slid toward $3,970. Her framing: 'Bitcoin has no CEO to lose.'
items.angle: The 'no key-man risk' pitch for BTC fails a live test: a $600B single-name shock in the index's biggest weight produced zero rotation into hard assets. Both BTC and gold fell, which says this is a liquidity and dollar story (DXY at a 19-month high, 10y at 5%), not a trust story.
items.tweetA: Nvidia just showed index investors what key-man risk looks like. The asset with 'no CEO to lose' fell anyway. BTC -2%, gold -1.5%, dollar at a 19-month high. When liquidity tightens, the hard-asset narrative waits its turn.
items.tweetB: Prediction markets had 88% odds Jensen was out before the board said a word, and they were right within days. The best-priced risk in this whole saga was on Polymarket/Kalshi, not on the sell-side desks still at Overweight.

items.title: Jobless claims 200K (+9K, 6K above consensus), but continuing claims fell to 1.697M vs ~1.9M last year

items.angle: With the 10y back above 5% after hot CPI and the Fed hiking, a labor market this tight takes away the usual excuse to cut. Continuing claims falling y/y is the opposite of what an AI-displacement story would predict, at least so far.
items.tweetA: Continuing claims 1.697M vs 1.9M a year ago. Everyone wants the AI-job-loss story to be in the data. It isn't. And a labor market this tight with the 10y at 5% means the Fed isn't coming to rescue the Nasdaq.
items.tweetB: 200K initial claims gets a 'miss' headline. The 4-week average didn't move and continuing claims fell. That's a labor market that just doesn't break, which is the worst news for anyone long duration.

items.title: OPEC+ quota producers added 1,945 kbpd in October and are now only 1.1 MMbpd below pre-Iran-war February
items.idea: Per OPEC's MOMR secondary sources, quota-participating crude rose 1,945 kbpd in October, led by Saudi Arabia and Iraq (Iraq now 300+ kbpd above February). Supply to market is only 1.1 MMbpd below February 2026, and Saudi Arabia's self-declared output closes that gap. Iranian production fell to its lowest since the 1980s under the US blockade.
items.angle: Gulf supply is effectively back while Iranian barrels sit at 40-year lows. Combine that with Trump saying 'no deal with Iran needed' (Mando) and the market loses the supply-return catalyst a deal was supposed to bring, because the barrels already returned through Saudi and Iraq.
items.tweetA: Iran's oil output is at its lowest since the 1980s. OPEC+ is 1.1 MMbpd from pre-war levels anyway. Saudi and Iraq quietly backfilled a war. That's why 'Iran deal' headlines barely move crude anymore.
items.tweetB: Iraq is producing 300 kbpd MORE than before the war started. Wars don't just take barrels offline; they hand market share to whoever can ship. Riyadh and Baghdad are the winners nobody is pricing.

items.title: Middle East implied production touched pre-war levels in late October, then fell back 3-4 MMbpd as Hormuz transits dropped
items.idea: Implied Middle East production briefly returned to roughly pre-war levels in late October before pulling back. At latest count it is 3-4 MMbpd below pre-war again after observed Hormuz transits fell. Johnston nets out unidentified Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers and says total liquid supply is looking 'durably tolerable', but the costs and tanker stress of these dark transits are 'unsustainably heavy.'
items.angle: The supply problem has turned into a freight-and-insurance problem. When dark STS transfers become the plumbing, tanker rates and war-risk premia (not flat price) are the cleaner way to express Hormuz risk.
items.tweetA: Hormuz flows went back to pre-war levels for a moment, then dropped 3-4 MMbpd again. The oil market has adapted to the war. The tanker market hasn't. If you want Hormuz exposure, it's in freight, not in Brent.
items.tweetB: Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship transfers are now material enough that a top oil analyst has to net them out of supply estimates. A dark fleet has become core infrastructure. That's a sanctions regime that has stopped working.

items.title: Census: data centre construction $96.5B/yr vs general offices $46.0B. Machines now get 2x the building that humans do
items.idea: The Census Bureau still files data centres under 'Office.' In 2014 the sub-line was $1.6B/yr; in September 2026 it ran at $96.5B, +90% y/y, versus $46.0B for offices with people in them. A year ago they were level, and the $50.5B gap is the widest on record. June to September added $24B, so data-centre construction now adds the whole of US office construction every 6 months.
items.angle: A 60x rise in 12 years is the run-rate input for electrical equipment, switchgear and construction labor. It's also a preliminary print growing 90% a year, the kind of series that gets revised and then mean-reverts.
items.tweetA: In 2014 US data centre construction was $1.6B/yr. Today it's $96.5B, 2x all office construction for humans. The Census still classifies it as 'Office.' Our statistics can't even name the boom they're measuring.
items.tweetB: Every 6 months, US data-centre construction adds the equivalent of ALL general office construction. Office building is 37% below its 2020 peak. Capital didn't leave real estate. It changed tenants from people to GPUs.

items.title: Ex-data-centres, US private non-residential construction is -4% y/y. Factories -18%. Only power (+14%) is growing
items.idea: Strip out data centres and private non-res construction is down ~4% y/y, with manufacturing -18%. The only other major line growing at pace is electric power, +14% to $147B. Churches are +21%, but off a $6B base. General office is 37% below its Feb 2020 peak, back at January 2016 levels.
items.angle: Reshoring has stalled: factories -18% is the opposite of the industrial-policy narrative. The capex economy is now a single bet on AI plus the grid it needs, which makes the whole construction cycle hostage to hyperscaler budgets.
items.tweetA: Factory construction -18% y/y. Remember reshoring? The entire US non-res construction cycle is now data centres plus the power plants to run them. Take those out and it's a recession.
items.tweetB: Construction growth in 2026: data centres +90%, power +14%, churches +21%, factories -18%. America is building for machines, electrons, and prayer.

items.title: Margin at every layer: TSMC 66%, Nvidia 75%, clouds 45% op, Anthropic 85% gross. Power is the only bottleneck
items.idea: Pal's 'First Law': systems maximise intelligence per unit of energy. AI capability cost falls ~10x a year, and nobody in the stack sells below cost. His contrast with 2000: telecoms laid fibre ahead of demand and only ~5% was lit by 2001, while this buildout faces 'infinite demand.' He still flags overshoot risk, since general office construction halved from $54.8B (Jan 2001) to $25.8B (Apr 2003), along with weak credits waiting on grid connections that may never come.
items.angle: Four layers each earning 45-85% margins on the same dollar of end demand is not a stable equilibrium. Someone's margin is the next layer's cost-reduction target, and SemiAnalysis is already saying Nvidia's suppliers will stop prioritising it.
items.tweetA: TSMC 66% gross. Nvidia 75%. Cloud 45% operating. Anthropic 85% gross. Four layers, all fat margins on the same end-user dollar. In every tech cycle I know, stacked margins like that get competed down from both ends.
items.tweetB: In 2001, 95% of the fibre laid was dark. Raoul's case is that this time demand exceeds supply. Fine, but office construction halved in 27 months after 2001 and that was a 'sure thing' too. The tell will be grid-connection queues, not chip orders.

items.title: Texas elected a governor who campaigned on a data-centre moratorium. Texas holds ~25% of the planned US build
items.idea: Per Wells Fargo (cited by Pal), Texas holds about a quarter of planned US data-centre construction, and its newly elected governor campaigned on a moratorium on new data centres. Pal's view is that a moratorium in one state just moves the build to the next. Separately, the TWIAI panel discussed the anti-data-centre movement's origins, including a Bitcoin Policy Institute report alleging foreign influence and a $5B Maryland project being blocked.
items.angle: This is the first time anti-data-centre politics has won statewide where the capacity actually is. Land with power and interconnect is not fungible across states on a 2-3 year horizon, so a Texas pause re-rates whoever already holds energized sites.
items.tweetA: The state with ~25% of America's planned data-centre build just elected a governor who ran on a moratorium. 'It'll just move to another state' assumes power and interconnect are fungible. They aren't. Energized land just got scarcer.
items.tweetB: Electricity bills just became a campaign issue that wins statewide in TEXAS. If the AI trade's binding constraint was power, it's now power plus politics. Data-centre REITs with energized sites are the quiet winners.

items.title: United Airlines blocks unauthorized third-party AI agents from booking. META -2%, EXPE/BKNG up
items.idea: Meta fell 2% Wednesday after United said it will restrict unauthorized third-party AI agents from its booking systems, a key use case for Meta's Muse agent. Expedia and Booking gained. blocmates frames it as United 'banning personal AI agents from booking flights.' Separately, The Telegraph reports banks banning AI from accounts over rogue-agent fears.
items.angle: This is the first big incumbent counterattack in the agent economy: whoever owns the inventory can wall it off. The OTAs, as authorised intermediaries, suddenly look like toll roads rather than roadkill.
items.tweetA: Bear case for AI agents in one headline: United just blocked them. The agent can be as smart as you like, but if the merchant won't let it in, the OTA middleman lives. $EXPE $BKNG up, $META down. Inventory owners hold the keys.
items.tweetB: Everyone modeled AI agents disintermediating Expedia. Nobody modeled airlines and banks simply blocking agents. Distribution moats came back the moment agents became a threat.

items.title: China approves Lilly's orforglipron: the first oral GLP-1 for weight management in China
items.idea: China's NMPA approved orforglipron for adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related comorbidity. It's the first oral GLP-1 approved in China for weight management. Also: QXO named Novelis CFO Dev Ahuja as CFO effective January 2027.
items.angle: Pill form removes the cold chain and injection barrier, which matters most in a market as large and price-sensitive as China. It also arrives just as Chinese biotechs push their own GLP-1s, so pricing will be the next fight.
items.tweetA: Lilly's oral GLP-1 just cleared China first among pills. No cold chain, no needle, 1.4B people. The obesity-drug TAM models were built on injectables in rich countries. Redo them. $LLY
items.tweetB: The interesting part of Lilly's China approval isn't Lilly. It's that a pill makes GLP-1 a mass-market consumer product in China, which hits packaged food and quick-service restaurants in the world's biggest consumer market.

items.title: 'Can it run Doom?' becomes 'Can it decompile Halo?' At least 4 AI-decompiled Halo instances already run in-browser
items.idea: AI agents are now good at taking games apart as well as building them. Per Jon Lai there are at least four decompiled Halo instances running in-browser. Maurice Heumann's agent-team FPS decompilation needed a verification harness that recompiled each function and compared it with the original binary. Xbox Labs is exploring reconstruction for new hardware, browser ports and remixes, and Tim Sweeney reorganised Epic around AI-assisted development.
items.angle: Mass automated decompilation turns every legacy back catalogue into either an IP-protection liability or a remaster pipeline. Platform holders with deep libraries (MSFT, Nintendo, Sony) gain optionality, and the legal fight over decompiled code is coming.

items.title: A 9,000-line microkernel vs Linux's 40M lines: the Ethereum Foundation launches a signing app on Foundation's KeyOS
items.idea: Foundation's KeyOS (on its $349 Passport Prime device) runs the Ethereum Foundation's new Universal Ethereum Signer, built by Ledger co-founder Nicolas Bacca. Each app gets a hardened child key, never the master seed. The ~9,000-line microkernel is auditable vs Linux's ~40M lines, with formal verification planned. Magic Backups split a seed into three Shamir shares across two NFC cards and a phone, with no email or username on file. Devices are built in an ITAR-certified US facility with active anti-tamper switches. Context from blocmates: a wave of hardware-wallet attacks shut down Sui wallet Suiball, and Ledger's CEO says 'everybody will be hacked at some point.'
items.angle: Security is moving from 'trust the vendor' to 'minimise the auditable surface', which is the same logic as formal verification of Signal by DeepMind agents this week. Small, verifiable kernels plus AI-driven verification could make hardware signers provably secure for the first time.
items.tweetA: Linux kernel: ~40M lines. Foundation's KeyOS: ~9,000. You can't audit 40M lines; you can formally verify 9,000, especially now that AI agents verify cryptographic protocols in weeks. Security is becoming a size problem.
items.tweetB: The Ethereum Foundation is shipping its own signing app, built by a Ledger co-founder, on a non-Ledger device made in an ITAR facility. Ledger's CEO says 'everybody will be hacked.' The hardware-wallet market is being rebuilt from the kernel up.
